finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $40-$111 (0.17-0.5 hr); midsize 2016 CR-V about $81-$110 (0.5 hr); truck 2016 F-150 about $52-$111 (0.25-0.5 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $81-$162 (0.5-0.75 hr). Posted menu prices for the filter alone run $24.99 to $78.88 at four sellers; three of the four are $25-$31, close to the price of the filter itself and below every built total, so many shops charge little or nothing for the labor when the filter is added to other work. A supportable range for the site is roughly $25-$110 for mainstream vehicles and up to about $160 for a European car. RepairPal ($79-$99 national, $67-$84 for one compact car) and Jerry ($73-$142) sit in the upper half of that; YourMechanic's $166 and up is a mobile visit charge and is not comparable to a shop adding the filter to other work. How solid the numbers are: the parts prices are firm for the genuine filter (list price $30-$42 on all four examples), but the low ends for the Corolla, CR-V and F-150 are discounted genuine parts, because no aftermarket price with confirmed fitment could be loaded; aftermarket filters are usually cheaper still (CR-V filters of unconfirmed year were $16-$25). The BMW part number is not confirmed for the 2015 328i sedan on the maker catalog page, and a second, dearer filter ($27-$39 aftermarket) is also listed for the 328i. The labor times are the weak part. No manufacturer bulletin, filter maker or trade-press article states a time for replacing one engine air filter: makers treat it as maintenance, not a warranty repair (the one GM bulletin found allows 0.5 hr to check the filter and reset a dash message on a 2019 Silverado). The truck times are a parts seller's install-time statements for single F-150 filters (15 and 30 minutes; one listing says 1 hour and is set aside as an outlier). The other three classes rest on a repair-manual publisher's do-it-yourself guides (Haynes): 10 minutes for a 2001-2004 Corolla, 30 minutes for the Toyota Auris and the 2012-2017 CR-V, 30-45 minutes for the BMW 3-Series. Those guide pages say 30 minutes or more in their summary table and '5-10 minutes' in their text, so they disagree with themselves; the table figures were used, which makes these totals an upper view of the labor. Neither economy figure is for the 2015 Corolla itself. All of these are owner-level install times, not flat-rate book times, and a shop that already has the hood open will take less. Menu prices came from 6 sellers (5 dealers, 1 independent) in 6 states; two of them bundle the cabin filter and are marked as a different service; no national chain prints a price for this service on the pages loaded. Confidence is low: no class has a maker or book labor time, the economy times are for comparable vehicles, and three of four low parts prices are a discounted genuine filter. Second attempt (2026-11-20): the first attempt's labor figures came from another estimator's consumer guide (Jerry); those were removed from the hours and kept only as a comparison in the benchmarks.
extras: This is usually sold alongside an oil change or a mileage service, not as its own visit, and it is often offered together with a cabin air filter (posted prices for both filters together: $137.99 to $169.95). A quote may add shop supplies and sales tax. Performance or washable filters cost far more than a standard paper element ($57-$114 on the listings seen). On a few engines the filter housing is harder to reach and the labor is higher.
